title: Theo's Amazing Apple Journey
markdown:
The sun popped over the garden fence as if it had somewhere to be. Theo stretched, a yawn escaping before he could give it a job. The day had begun with an apple: big, crisp, red, still cool from the bowl. He bit. Crunch. Juice did the rest, a bright splash that made the morning feel already paid for.

“This is ripe enough to taste like it remembers the tree,” he told the fence, which had no opinion and a great deal of lichen.

Ash the lizard, on a warm stone, flicked his tail and blinked those quick bright eyes. He had watched birds take seeds, ants ferry crumbs, and now Theo reducing a fruit to a smaller and smaller argument. “Where does it go? Does it vanish? I have looked in your pockets. No apple.”

Theo paused, juice on his chin, and wiped a sticky smear across the back of his hand. “I eat it. It feels good. Then — inside?” He poked his tummy, which had no immediate answers and a faint professional rumble, as if a factory had heard its name.

Engineer Mara zipped past along the path, toolbox rattling, goggles glinting, curly hair bouncing as if it had its own project and a deadline. She stopped so neatly the spanners kept a polite silence. “A food route. Morning’s a good time for one. We trace it. Garden stations, if you like maps.”

She tapped the spanner against her palm, tick, and pointed first at Theo’s mouth as if it were a gate. “Every bite starts a construction job. Body as building. Food as fuel. First stop: the mouth. Teeth as demolition — crunch, grind, smaller bits. The tongue mixes. Saliva is the liquid that begins the breakdown so the swallow is soft instead of a dare.”

Theo pictured wrecking balls and a whisk and did not say the picture aloud, because Ash was already taking notes with his whole face, throat pulsing. Theo chewed the next bite slower, feeling the grind, the wet, the sudden ease.

“Then the oesophagus.” Mara walked them as far as the water butt, which would have to stand in for a tunnel. “A muscular tube. One-way. Gentle squeezes, like toothpaste, down to the next station. No debating in the dark. The mush does not get a vote.”

They imagined the apple, still faintly pink, travelling that smooth slide. Ash wiggled his nose. Scales caught sun. “Where next? I would like a signpost.”

“Stomach.” She rapped the compost bin, kindly. “Strong flexible bag. Churns. Mixes with digestive juices. The apple becomes soup that has forgotten it was a fruit. A small factory that does not take weekends and does not send postcards.”

Theo patted the rumble. “Working. I can hear the shift.”

“Then the important stretch.” Mara led them along the bean row, which coiled enough to suggest the idea. “The small intestine. Long, coiled, narrow, lined with villi — tiny finger-like bits. They take the useful cargo, vitamins, sugars, energy, and pass it to the blood. Delivery to brain, muscle, toes. That is the dash-and-climb-and-bask fund. Without villi you would have a very expensive chew and nowhere for the pay to go.”

Ash’s eyes went wider and greener. “So that is the power. Not the crunch. The handover.”

“What remains goes to the large intestine.” The far fence, wider in the telling than in timber. “Wider, shorter. Water pulled back so the body does not waste it. The rest packed for the last trip out. A recycling plant with no speeches and a very honest exit.”

Theo looked from Ash to Mara, apple still in hand, route now a list he could walk. “Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. A team. If one station slacks, the others inherit a mess.”

“Digestive system,” Mara said. “Breaks food down, extracts the fuel, keeps a day like this from running on empty. You were already using it. Now you can draw it.”

Theo took another crisp bite, sweetness as evidence, and felt — or decided he felt — a faint tingle that might have been sugar starting its commute. He did not declare the morning a wonder of the age. He logged crunch / swallow-slide / villi-delivery in the garden book, left the core for the compost where cores belong, and let Ash inspect the warm stone as if it were a second stomach he declined to use. The sun, having popped the fence, stayed up. Theo’s toes, newly funded, were ready to be toes, and he used them to walk the bean row once more, naming each station under his breath so the apple would not get lost for lack of a map.
